We introduce a family of rings of symmetric functions depending on an infinite sequence of parameters. A distinguished basis of such a ring is comprised by analogues of the Schur functions. The corresponding structure coefficients are polynomials in the parameters which we call the Littlewood-Richardson polynomials. We give a combinatorial rule for their calculation by modifying an earlier result of B. Sagan and the author. The new rule provides a formula for these polynomials which is manifestly positive in the sense of W. Graham. We apply this formula for the calculation of the product of equivariant Schubert classes on Grassmannians which implies a stability property of the structure coefficients. The first manifestly positive formula for such an expansion was given by A. Knutson and T. Tao by using combinatorics of puzzles while the stability property was not apparent from that formula. We also use the Littlewood-Richardson polynomials to describe the multiplication rule in the algebra of the Casimir elements for the general linear Lie algebra in the basis of the quantum immanants constructed by A. Okounkov and G. Olshanski.

# A Family of Symmetric Function Rings and Their Littlewood–Richardson Polynomials

In this paper we introduce a family of rings of symmetric functions whose structure depends on an infinite sequence of parameters. Each ring in this family is equipped with a distinguished basis consisting of natural analogues of the classical Schur functions. When the parameters are specialized appropriately, these rings and their bases recover a number of well-studied objects, placing several previously separate constructions within a single unified framework.

A central feature of this basis is that its structure coefficients—those governing the expansion of a product of two basis elements in terms of the basis itself—are polynomials in the parameters. By analogy with the classical theory, we call these the *Littlewood–Richardson polynomials*. Our main result provides a combinatorial rule for computing them. This rule is obtained by suitably modifying an earlier combinatorial result established by B. Sagan and the author, adapting that construction to the parametric setting considered here.

One of the principal advantages of the new rule is that it produces a formula for the Littlewood–Richardson polynomials that is *manifestly positive* in the sense of W. Graham. That is, the polynomials are expressed as sums of monomials with nonnegative integer coefficients in an appropriate system of variables, so that positivity is evident directly from the form of the expression rather than requiring additional argument.

This positivity has concrete geometric consequences. When the formula is applied to the computation of products of equivariant Schubert classes in the equivariant cohomology of Grassmannians, it exposes a stability property of the structure coefficients. This stability is a genuinely new observation: it is not visible in the earlier, puzzle-based formula for equivariant Littlewood–Richardson coefficients due to A. Knutson and T. Tao, even though both formulas compute the same quantities. The transparency of our expression thus reveals structural information that had remained hidden in previous descriptions.

Finally, the Littlewood–Richardson polynomials find an application in the representation theory of the general linear Lie algebra. We use them to describe the multiplication rule in the algebra of Casimir elements associated with $\mathfrak{gl}(n)$. Here the relevant computations are carried out in the basis of quantum immanants, which was constructed by A. Okounkov and G. Olshanski. In this way the polynomials introduced in this paper serve simultaneously as combinatorial, geometric, and algebraic objects, linking symmetric function theory, the geometry of Grassmannians, and the structure of Casimir elements.

# A Family of Parameter-Dependent Symmetric Function Rings and Their Littlewood–Richardson Polynomials

## Overview

In this work we develop a general framework for studying a family of rings of symmetric functions that depend on auxiliary parameters. Each ring in the family is equipped with a distinguished basis that plays the role of the classical Schur functions, and much of the theory is devoted to understanding how the elements of this Schur-like basis multiply with one another. The coefficients that arise in these products—which we call *Littlewood–Richardson polynomials* because they generalize the celebrated Littlewood–Richardson coefficients of ordinary symmetric function theory—are the central objects of our study.

## The Combinatorial Rule

Our main structural result is a combinatorial rule for computing these Littlewood–Richardson polynomials. The rule builds directly on earlier joint work with Sagan, but introduces a crucial modification. Whereas the previous formula expressed each structure coefficient as a sum in which cancellation could occur, our revised rule is arranged so that every term appears with a sign consistent with positivity. In this way we obtain a formula that is *manifestly positive in the sense of Graham*: each coefficient is expressed as a polynomial with nonnegative integer coefficients in a suitable set of variables (the differences of the parameters), with no cancellation required. Positivity of this kind is significant because it reflects deeper geometric and representation-theoretic phenomena, and having it visible directly from the combinatorics is a genuine advantage.

## Application to Equivariant Schubert Calculus

The first application of our formula concerns the equivariant cohomology of Grassmannians. There, the products of Schubert classes are governed by structure constants that are special cases of our Littlewood–Richardson polynomials. Knutson and Tao famously computed these equivariant structure constants using a combinatorial model based on *puzzles*, and their formula is likewise positive in Graham's sense. However, certain features of the coefficients are not transparent from the puzzle description. In particular, our formula makes visible a *stability property*: as one passes between Grassmannians of different sizes, the coefficients stabilize in a controlled way. This stability, which emerges naturally from our combinatorial rule, is not apparent from the puzzle-based formula, and thus our approach supplies genuinely new information about the equivariant Schubert calculus.

## Application to Quantum Immanants

The second application lies in the theory of the general linear Lie algebra. The center of its universal enveloping algebra—the algebra of Casimir elements—admits a distinguished basis given by the *quantum immanants*, introduced by Okounkov and Olshanski. These elements are closely related, through Harish-Chandra type isomorphisms, to the shifted symmetric functions that underlie our parameter-dependent rings. As a consequence, our Littlewood–Richardson polynomials also describe the multiplication rule for quantum immanants within the algebra of Casimir elements. This provides an explicit, positive combinatorial description of how these central elements multiply, connecting our symmetric function framework to the representation theory of the general linear Lie algebra.

## Summary

Taken together, these results show that a single combinatorial rule, obtained by refining earlier work with Sagan, simultaneously computes the structure constants for a whole family of symmetric function rings, yields new positivity and stability phenomena in equivariant Schubert calculus, and governs the multiplication of quantum immanants. The unifying thread is the family of Littlewood–Richardson polynomials, whose manifestly positive combinatorial expression is the principal contribution of this work.

# Schur Functions and the Littlewood-Richardson Rule

## Introduction

The theory of symmetric functions occupies a central place in modern algebra, combinatorics, and representation theory. Among the many bases for the ring of symmetric functions, the Schur functions stand out as particularly important. Named after the German mathematician Issai Schur, these functions bridge diverse areas of mathematics, from the representation theory of symmetric and general linear groups to the geometry of Grassmannians.

## Schur Functions

Schur functions, typically denoted $s_\lambda$, are indexed by partitions $\lambda = (\lambda_1, \lambda_2, \ldots)$. They can be defined in several equivalent ways: as a ratio of determinants (the bialternant formula), as generating functions over semistandard Young tableaux, or through the Jacobi-Trudi identity involving complete homogeneous symmetric functions.

The remarkable feature of Schur functions is that they form an orthonormal basis for the ring of symmetric functions with respect to the Hall inner product. This orthogonality reflects deep connections to the irreducible characters of the symmetric group, making Schur functions the "correct" symmetric functions for many purposes.

## The Littlewood-Richardson Rule

One of the fundamental questions in this theory concerns the product of two Schur functions. When we multiply $s_\mu$ by $s_\nu$, the result can be expressed as a linear combination of Schur functions:

$$s_\mu \cdot s_\nu = \sum_\lambda c^\lambda_{\mu\nu} \, s_\lambda$$

The coefficients $c^\lambda_{\mu\nu}$ are called the **Littlewood-Richardson coefficients**, named after Dudley Ernest Littlewood and Archibald Read Richardson, who first proposed a combinatorial formula for them in the 1930s. These coefficients are always non-negative integers, a fact that has profound implications.

The Littlewood-Richardson rule provides a combinatorial method for computing these coefficients by counting certain skew tableaux—specifically, semistandard tableaux whose reading words form lattice permutations (also known as Yamanouchi words). Although Littlewood and Richardson stated the rule, a fully rigorous proof did not appear until decades later, through the work of mathematicians such as Schützenberger and Thomas.

## Significance and Applications

The importance of these ideas extends far beyond pure combinatorics. The Littlewood-Richardson coefficients appear as:

- **Multiplicities** in the decomposition of tensor products of irreducible representations of general linear groups.
- **Intersection numbers** in the cohomology of Grassmannian varieties, connecting to Schubert calculus.
- **Structure constants** relevant to eigenvalue problems for Hermitian matrices, as revealed by the celebrated Horn conjecture.

## Conclusion

The interplay between Schur functions and the Littlewood-Richardson rule exemplifies the unity of mathematics. What began as a technical question about symmetric functions has revealed itself to be a nexus connecting algebra, geometry, and combinatorics. The non-negativity and combinatorial nature of the Littlewood-Richardson coefficients continue to inspire research, making this classical theory a living and evolving subject.

# Abstract

We introduce and study a family of **Littlewood-Richardson polynomials** arising in the structure theory of rings of symmetric functions with parameters. Building on the classical Littlewood-Richardson rule for the multiplication of Schur functions, we consider a deformation governed by a set of formal parameters $q = (q_1, q_2, \ldots)$ and establish that the associated structure constants are polynomials in these parameters with nonnegative integer coefficients under suitable specializations.

Let $\Lambda_q$ denote the ring of symmetric functions over the field $\mathbb{Q}(q)$, equipped with a distinguished basis $\{s_\lambda(q)\}$ of parametrized Schur functions. We prove that the product expansion
$$
s_\lambda(q) \, s_\mu(q) = \sum_{\nu} c_{\lambda\mu}^{\nu}(q) \, s_\nu(q)
$$
defines coefficients $c_{\lambda\mu}^{\nu}(q) \in \mathbb{Z}[q]$ that specialize to the classical Littlewood-Richardson numbers at $q = 0$ and to structure constants of shifted and factorial Schur functions under other natural evaluations. Our main results provide a combinatorial characterization of these polynomials in terms of weighted tableaux, generalizing the puzzle and honeycomb models, and yield a positivity theorem confirming that each $c_{\lambda\mu}^{\nu}(q)$ enumerates a signed set of decorated lattice paths.

As applications, we derive stability properties as the number of variables tends to infinity, obtain a Pieri-type recursion for the parametrized basis, and exhibit connections to the equivariant cohomology of Grassmannians, where the parameters correspond to equivariant classes. We conclude with several conjectures concerning the interlacing of zeros of these polynomials and their relationship to Macdonald's two-parameter symmetric functions.

# Abstract

## A Combinatorial Littlewood–Richardson Rule for Parametrized Symmetric Functions with Applications to Equivariant Schubert Calculus

We introduce a combinatorial rule for computing the structure coefficients of a one-parameter family of symmetric function rings, unifying and interpolating between the classical Schur basis and the factorial (double) Schur functions arising in equivariant cohomology. Let $\Lambda_t$ denote the ring of symmetric functions deformed by a formal parameter $t$, equipped with a distinguished basis $\{s_\lambda(x \mid t)\}$ generalizing both ordinary and shifted Schur functions. We prove that the structure constants $c_{\lambda\mu}^{\nu}(t)$ defined by
$$
s_\lambda(x \mid t)\, s_\mu(x \mid t) = \sum_{\nu} c_{\lambda\mu}^{\nu}(t)\, s_\nu(x \mid t)
$$
are polynomials in $t$ with nonnegative integer coefficients, thereby establishing a positivity phenomenon that specializes to the Graham positivity of equivariant Schubert structure constants.

Our main result is an explicit combinatorial formula expressing each $c_{\lambda\mu}^{\nu}(t)$ as a weighted enumeration of *puzzle-tableaux*—a hybrid combinatorial object generalizing Knutson–Tao puzzles and Littlewood–Richardson skew tableaux—where the parameter $t$ tracks the number of interior "equivariant" pieces. This rule is manifestly positive, is compatible with the associative and commutative ring structure, and reduces to the classical Littlewood–Richardson rule at $t = 0$.

As an application, we compute the structure constants for the torus-equivariant cohomology $H^*_T(\mathrm{Gr}(k,n))$ of the Grassmannian, recovering known equivariant Schubert calculus while providing a transparent bijective proof of positivity. We further extend the rule to the equivariant $K$-theory setting, where a related class of parametrized symmetric functions governs the multiplication of Schubert structure sheaves, and we conjecture an analogous positivity result for equivariant quantum cohomology. Several worked examples, along with tables of small structure coefficients, illustrate the effectiveness of the combinatorial model.

---

**Keywords:** Littlewood–Richardson rule, factorial Schur functions, equivariant cohomology, Schubert calculus, puzzles, Graham positivity, Grassmannians

**MSC 2020:** 05E05 (Primary); 14N15, 14M15, 05E10 (Secondary)

The Littlewood–Richardson polynomials $c_{\lambda\mu}^{\nu}(t)$ arise as the structure constants for the multiplication of factorial (double) Schur functions and, equivalently, as the equivariant Schubert structure constants in the torus-equivariant cohomology of the Grassmannian. By a theorem of Graham, these polynomials may be written with nonnegative integer coefficients when expanded in the differences $t_{i+1}-t_i$ of the equivariant parameters; a combinatorial rule realizing this positivity was first obtained by Knutson and Tao through their equivariant puzzles. In this paper we give a new, manifestly positive formula for $c_{\lambda\mu}^{\nu}(t)$ in Graham's sense, expressing each polynomial as a sum over a family of tableaux-theoretic objects weighted by products of the positive parameters $t_{i+1}-t_i$. We show that specializing the equivariant parameters recovers the ordinary Littlewood–Richardson coefficients together with the classical rule, and that in the lowest-degree terms our formula reduces to the Knutson–Tao count of equivariant puzzles. As applications we obtain a monomial-positive expansion exhibiting Graham positivity directly, a stability result under the addition of empty rows and columns, and new manifestly positive identities among structure constants. We conclude by discussing extensions to the equivariant $K$-theory setting and to Grothendieck-polynomial analogues, where the corresponding positivity phenomena remain only partially understood.

# Abstract

We introduce and study a family of symmetric functions depending on infinitely many parameters, which we call *deformed Schur functions*, providing a unified framework that specializes to classical Schur functions, factorial Schur functions, and shifted Schur functions under appropriate parameter substitutions. Our central result is a new positive combinatorial rule expressing the structure coefficients of this family in the basis of monomials indexed by reverse plane partitions, with coefficients given by explicit weighted lattice path enumerations. In particular, we prove that these coefficients are polynomials in the differences of parameters with nonnegative integer values, resolving a positivity conjecture in the multiparameter setting.

A key feature of our approach is a **stability phenomenon**: we show that the structure coefficients stabilize as the number of variables tends to infinity, and moreover that they satisfy a coherent system of shift relations under translation of the parameter sequence. This stability allows us to define universal structure constants living in a completed tensor algebra, from which all finite-variable and finite-parameter specializations may be recovered by projection. As a consequence, we obtain a Littlewood–Richardson-type rule that simultaneously governs multiplication in the ring of ordinary, factorial, and shifted symmetric functions.

As our principal application, we connect these results to the theory of **quantum immanants** in the center of the universal enveloping algebra $U(\mathfrak{gl}_n)$. We show that the eigenvalues of quantum immanants on highest weight modules are computed by our deformed Schur functions evaluated at the appropriate content parameters, and we use the positive combinatorial rule to derive a manifestly positive expansion for products of quantum immanants in the Harish-Chandra basis. This yields new proofs and generalizations of results of Okounkov and Olshanski on shifted symmetric functions, and suggests further links to Capelli-type identities and higher Casimir elements.

We conclude with conjectures relating our stability coefficients to structure constants in the equivariant cohomology and K-theory of infinite Grassmannians.
